chief_complaint: severe wave-like flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria
hpi_details: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe wave-like flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he tore a deep muscle or ruptured an internal organ while lifting heavy weights at the gym.
concerns: He is afraid that seeing blood in his urine means his kidney has suffered permanent damage or that he will need emergency surgery.
expectations: He hopes to get immediate strong pain relief and an imaging scan to see exactly where the bleeding is coming from.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Ureteral Calculus (Renal Colic) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Suspected renal colic requires prompt identification of infected obstruction, anuria/AKI, solitary kidney, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, or an alternative emergency diagnosis.

Obtain vital signs, urinalysis with culture when infection is possible, and creatinine; use appropriate imaging to confirm stone location/size and obstruction. Hematuria alone does not determine composition.
NSAIDs are first-line analgesia only when renal, GI bleeding, anticoagulant, and allergy risks permit. Do not force fluids during acute colic.
Medical expulsive therapy is selective—not automatic—and should be discussed for suitable ureteral stones with orthostasis counseling and planned follow-up to document passage.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe wave-like flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria

Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe wave-like flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain vital signs, abdominal/CVA examination, urinalysis with culture if indicated, renal function, and imaging appropriate to risk; do not assume calcium composition before analysis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ureteral Calculus (Renal Colic).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute pyelonephritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Missing fever, rigors, sepsis physiology, or pyuria with obstruction, which requires urgent antibiotics and urologic decompression.
Missing anuria, AKI, solitary kidney, refractory vomiting/dehydration, or uncontrolled pain.
Giving NSAIDs or tamsulosin without contraindication and orthostasis review, or treating unconfirmed renal colic as a calcium stone.
management_principles: Stabilize, treat pain/nausea safely, obtain urine/renal testing and imaging, and urgently involve urology for complicated obstruction.
For an uncomplicated small ureteral stone, provide strainer, normal hydration as tolerated, selective MET counseling, and follow-up to confirm passage.
Send retrieved stones for analysis; address prevention only after composition and recurrence risk are known.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Severe wave-like flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria is suspicious for ureteral stone; fatigue requires infection/systemic-illness screening.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, abdominal/CVA examination, urinalysis/culture when indicated, creatinine, and appropriate imaging to define stone/obstruction.
reference_soap.assessment: Suspected ureteral calculus; urgently exclude infected obstruction and other emergencies. Stone composition is not known.
reference_soap.plan: Provide NSAID analgesia and antiemetic if safe, obtain testing/imaging, and urgently involve urology for infection with obstruction, anuria/AKI, solitary kidney, refractory vomiting, or uncontrolled pain. For uncomplicated stones, use a strainer, normal hydration as tolerated, selective MET counseling, and follow-up to confirm passage.

teaching.one_liner: Acute obstruction of the ureter by a kidney stone, producing severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria.

must_ask.objective: Colicky flank pain character and radiation
must_ask.say: Does the excruciating flank pain come in severe waves and shoot down into your groin or labia?
Have you noticed pink, red, or tea-colored urine when you go to the bathroom?
Do you feel extremely nauseous or vomit when the pain peaks?

must_ask.objective: Personal or family kidney stone history
must_ask.say: Have you or anyone in your family passed a kidney stone in the past?
Do you have high fever, shaking chills, or confusion right now?

history.answer: My right flank has been hurting with severe, squeezing wave-like pain since this morning, and my urine looks reddish.
It started suddenly early this morning and has been getting steadily worse over the past several hours.
It began deep in my right flank and lower back, and the spasms feel like they travel down toward my right groin.
Yes, the pain radiates straight down from my right side into my lower abdomen and groin area.
It feels like intense, squeezing cramps that come and go in severe waves rather than a steady ache.
During the worst spasms, the pain peaks at an 8 or 9 out of 10. It is unbearable when the wave hits.
Nothing seems to help. I cannot find any comfortable position and keep moving around trying to ease it.
No, I have never had any pain like this before in my life.
I felt very nauseated when the pain peaked and dry-heaved a couple of times, but I haven't vomited anything.
My bowel movements have been completely normal, with no diarrhea, constipation, or blood in my stool.
No, I haven't had any fever, shaking chills, or hot flashes.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and my stool has its normal brown color.
I noticed my urine turned a pinkish-red color this morning, but I haven't felt burning when urinating or had frequent urges.
I feel completely worn out from the pain, but I haven't passed out, lost consciousness, or felt faint.
No, I have no chest tightness, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
I had a normal home-cooked dinner last night, nothing particularly greasy or unusual, and I haven't had alcohol in over a week.
I took one ibuprofen tablet about two hours ago, but it did not relieve the pain at all.
No, I have never had heart rhythm problems, heart palpitations, or any blood vessel disease.
I feel completely drained and exhausted since this morning because the severe pain has been wearing me down.
I have still been able to produce urine without difficulty, and as far as I know, both of my kidneys are normal.
I thought I must have torn a deep muscle or ruptured something inside my back when I was working out at the gym.
Seeing blood in my urine really freaked me out, and I'm terrified that one of my kidneys is permanently damaged or bleeding internally.
I just need something strong right now to stop this agonizing pain and a scan to see what's bleeding inside me.
I have no history of chronic medical conditions, high blood pressure, or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter remedies, or nutritional supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink socially, having a beer or two maybe once or twice a month.
I am a graduate student living in an apartment with a roommate.
My father had a kidney stone in his forties, but there is no family history of kidney disease or other major illnesses.
I am sexually active with one female partner, consistently use protection, and have never had a sexually transmitted infection.

exam.finding: The patient is acutely uncomfortable, restless, and shifting frequently on the examination table due to pain.
Blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, pulse 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no visible distension, surgical scars, or skin discoloration.
Normoactive bowel sounds are present in all four quadrants with no abdominal bruits.
The abdomen is soft and non-tender to light and deep palpation without guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is elicited across any abdominal quadrant.
Negative Murphy's sign with no tenderness or inspiratory arrest during right upper quadrant palpation.
No tenderness at McBurney's point; Rovsing's, psoas, and obturator signs are negative.
Marked percussion tenderness over the right costovertebral angle; no tenderness on the left side.
Normal external genitalia with symmetric, non-tender testicles, no masses, and intact cremasteric reflexes bilaterally.
